title: Ponerse and Quedarse: The Change and What Stays

sections.content: You know *ponerse* from B1 Unit 25 and B1 Unit 39: a sudden, temporary change of mood, health or looks (*se puso pálido*). You also know *quedarse* from B1 Unit 39: the state that is left after something happens (*se quedó sin trabajo*). At B2 you use them together, because one event often has both parts. *Ponerse* is the change itself, the moment you go red or nervous. *Quedarse* is where you end up afterwards: *Se puso pálido y se quedó callado*. A cause can also be the subject, and the person becomes the object: *La noticia nos puso tristes* (the news made us sad).

sections.title: The change and the state that stays
rows: Se puso nerviosa antes del examen.
She got nervous before the exam. (the change)
Se quedó callada durante toda la cena.
She stayed quiet for the whole dinner. (the state)
La noticia nos puso muy tristes.
The news made us very sad. (the cause is the subject)
Los trabajadores se quedaron sin empleo.
The workers were left without jobs. (the result)
Al ver el precio, se puso pálido y se quedó sin palabras.
On seeing the price, he turned pale and was left speechless. (both)

items.spanish: Mi hermano se puso rojo de vergüenza.
items.english: My brother went red with embarrassment.

items.spanish: Cuando entró el jefe, todos nos quedamos callados.
items.english: When the boss came in, we all fell silent.

sections.content: Do not mix up *ponerse* + adjective (*se puso triste*, she became sad) with *ponerse a* from A2 Unit 32 (*se puso a llorar*, she started to cry). And with *quedarse* the adjective or *sin* + noun tells you what is left: *quedarse callado*, *quedarse sin dinero*.
